title: Recovery
lead: Failure models, STEAL/FORCE policies, write-ahead logging and ARIES phases.

sections.title: Failures and recovery responsibilities
sections.html:
Recovery’s required outcome

Recovery supports atomicity and durability and restores a state compatible with the transaction guarantees. In the timeline, T1,T2,T3 committed before the crash and must survive; active T4,T5 must leave no accepted partial effects. It is not enough to load whichever dirty pages happened to reach disk.

PDF pp. 1–3

Failure classes and normal-time preparation

Transaction failures include application/constraint errors and DBMS-forced aborts such as deadlock victims. System failures include software exceptions and machine/power crashes. The fail-stop model assumes non-volatile contents are not corrupted by that crash. Media failures destroy persistent data and require an archive, backup or replica; a log on the destroyed device is not an independent recovery copy.

Recovery has two parts: record sufficient information during normal processing, then reconstruct an acceptable state after failure. Pages are read into fast volatile buffers, changed there and eventually flushed. Acknowledged commits must survive despite losing memory; aborted partial work must not remain accepted even if some dirty pages were written earlier.

PDF pp. 4–6

sections.title: STEAL and FORCE policies
sections.html:
STEAL and FORCE are independent choices

STEAL allows flushing a dirty page containing uncommitted updates when replacing a buffer frame; NO-STEAL forbids it. FORCE requires all transaction data updates on stable storage before commit; NO-FORCE does not. Replacement permission and commit-time persistence are different decisions. Neither term describes whether log records are durable.

PDF p. 7

NO-STEAL/FORCE source trace

Disk starts A=1,B=9,C=7. T1 changes A to 3 in memory, while T2 changes B to 8. Before T2 commits, memory is (3,8,7) and disk remains (1,9,7). NO-STEAL prevents persisting T1’s uncommitted A=3. T2’s FORCE commit persists B=8, yielding disk (1,8,7). When T1 aborts, restoring or discarding its private change returns memory A to 1.

This explains every stage of the repeated figure: initial state; first write; second transaction begins; second write; policy annotations; B forced; A rolled back. If two transactions modify the same physical page, a real implementation must preserve the rule at page granularity rather than blindly flushing another transaction’s uncommitted bytes.

PDF pp. 8–14

Costs and the atomic-flush caveat

In the simplified model NO-STEAL avoids disk UNDO and FORCE avoids REDO of committed pages. It needs room for all uncommitted dirty pages and can force many random writes. It still needs a mechanism to survive a crash halfway through forcing several pages: FORCE by itself is not an atomic multi-page commit protocol.

PDF p. 15

sections.title: UNDO, REDO and logging
sections.html:
Why STEAL needs UNDO and NO-FORCE needs REDO

If an uncommitted page reaches disk and its transaction aborts or the system crashes, restore the old state: UNDO. If commit is acknowledged while a changed page remains only in memory, a crash loses it unless the system can reapply the change: REDO.

PolicyFORCENO-FORCE
NO-STEALNo page-level UNDO/REDO in the simplified modelREDO required
STEALUNDO requiredUNDO and REDO required

STEAL/NO-FORCE permits useful replacement and defers random data writes, at the cost of both recovery obligations. A separate sequential log stores update differences and sufficient old/new information. Stable log storage and correct ordering are assumptions that must be implemented. The table abstracts page UNDO/REDO requirements and does not remove the multi-page atomicity caveat above.

PDF pp. 16–18

sections.title: Write-ahead logging rules
sections.html:
The two WAL ordering rules

First, persist every relevant update log record before its dirty data page is persisted; this makes earlier uncommitted data writes undoable. Second, persist the transaction’s records including COMMIT before reporting successful commit; this makes changes redoable even if data pages are not forced. Appending to a volatile log buffer is not equivalent to flushing stable storage. WAL orders log versus data and commit acknowledgment, not “force all data at every commit.”

PDF p. 19

WAL trace: A 1→8 and B 5→9

Start disk and buffer at A=1,B=5,C=7. BEGIN is logged; W(A) appends the old/new pair (1,8) and changes memory A to 8; W(B) appends (5,9) and changes memory B to 9. At commit, flush the log through its COMMIT record before responding:

001: <T1, BEGIN>
002: <T1, A, 1, 8>
003: <T1, B, 5, 9>
004: <T1, COMMIT>

The source crashes with disk still (1,5,7) and the committed log durable. REDO can restore (8,9,7). Had T1 not committed but its A page reached disk after the corresponding log flush, UNDO would restore A=1. Log sequence numbers identify order, not transaction data values.

PDF pp. 20–24

sections.title: ARIES analysis, redo and undo
sections.html:
ARIES: analysis, repeat history, undo

ARIES supports STEAL/NO-FORCE with WAL. Analysis scans from a checkpoint to reconstruct active transactions and dirty-page information. Redo starts at an appropriate log position and repeats history, including logged updates of transactions that may later be undone. Undo then reverses incomplete transactions.

Repeating history first reconstructs the state on which rollback must operate; it is not “redo only winners.” This source presents the three-phase outline, not the complete ARIES algorithms for pageLSNs, compensation log records and repeated crashes. Those additional mechanisms are necessary in a full implementation. Recovery correctness depends on the normal-time WAL rules as well as restart actions.

PDF pp. 25–27

quiz.question: What does STEAL + NO-FORCE typically require?
quiz.explanation: STEAL can put uncommitted data on disk, while NO-FORCE can leave committed data only in RAM.

source.summary: Lecture 21 connects buffer policies to recovery, explains WAL, and introduces the three ARIES phases: analysis, redo, and undo.

limitations: The lecture introduces ARIES at a high level; it is not a complete implementation specification.
